opus-5.5.text:
Around 2017, I'd say the field was in an interesting transitional moment. Deep learning had just transformed computer vision and was starting to make waves in other areas, and robotics was trying to figure out what that meant for us.

There were roughly two camps. On one side, you had the more traditional robotics mindset: model-based approaches, careful state estimation, motion planning, control theory. People in that camp were often skeptical of learning, and for good reasons. Robots operate in the physical world, failures are costly, and you want guarantees. Learning methods were seen as data-hungry, brittle, and hard to interpret.

On the other side, there was a lot of excitement coming from deep reinforcement learning. DeepMind's Atari results and AlphaGo had happened, and people were asking whether we could just learn policies end to end, from pixels to torques. There was some impressive work on visuomotor policies and large-scale grasping with many robots collecting data in parallel. The implicit belief there was that with enough data and the right algorithm, you could learn everything from scratch.

What I felt was missing, and what a lot of my PhD work grew out of, was the middle ground. Pure end-to-end RL was very sample-inefficient and struggled with long-horizon tasks, things that involve many steps and some sort of compositional structure, like assembling something or cooking. Classical methods handled structure well but didn't generalize to messy, unstructured environments. So the question I cared about was: how do we build in the right structure, like hierarchy, compositionality, or learning from demonstrations, so that learning becomes tractable for complex, multi-step tasks?

Imitation learning was also somewhat underappreciated at the time. RL got most of the attention, and imitation was sometimes viewed as the less principled cousin. Looking back, it's been quite striking to see how much the field has shifted toward learning from demonstrations at scale. But in 2017, that wasn't the obvious bet.

r001.rationale: The response describes traditional structured methods and advocates adding structure, but it does not identify a prevailing expectation to incorporate as much prior structure as possible.

r002.rationale: It says imitation learning was underappreciated while end-to-end RL was exciting, but does not connect the disparagement of supervised learning to an expectation that robots should learn by themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Around 2017 there were really two camps, and they didn't talk to each other as much as they should have.

On one side you had the classical robotics community, where the default assumption was that learning was fragile. You'd model the dynamics, you'd do planning, you'd do control, and if you used learning at all it was for perception, maybe a detector or a pose estimator sitting at the front of a very hand-engineered pipeline. The policy itself was something you designed. Learning the behavior end-to-end felt like giving up the guarantees that made robotics a serious engineering discipline.

On the other side, you had the deep learning and reinforcement learning excitement spilling over from vision and from games. People were seeing Atari and AlphaGo and thinking, okay, we just need to put a robot in the loop and run enough episodes. There was a lot of faith that reinforcement learning from scratch, with enough compute and enough simulation, would just work. And that was also partly wrong, because real robots are slow, reset is expensive, reward design is painful, and the sim-to-real gap was much bigger than people wanted to admit.

Where I was sitting, at Stanford, the question I kept coming back to was: where does the data come from? That was the thing both camps underrated. The RL folks assumed the robot would generate its own data through exploration. The classical folks assumed you didn't need much data at all. Imitation learning, learning from demonstrations, was kind of unfashionable in between. It was seen as a crutch, something you'd use to bootstrap and then throw away.

But my view was that human demonstrations were actually the most reliable source of signal we had, and the real research question was how to structure the learning so that a modest number of demonstrations could generalize. That's where things like learning task structure, hierarchical representations, and later large-scale teleoperation came from. So I'd say the prevailing mindset in 2017 was polarized between "learning is for perception only" and "RL will solve everything," and the data-centric, imitation-first view that ended up driving a lot of what came later was still a minority position.

r001.rationale: It describes hand-engineered pipelines and designed policies, but does not identify a prevailing principle that systems should incorporate as much prior structure as possible.

r002.rationale: It says RL researchers expected robots to generate data through exploration and that imitation learning was unfashionable, but does not clearly state that the self-learning expectation was why supervised learning was disparaged.

astra-6.text:
Around 2017, I’d characterize it as a divide between two mindsets. One was the traditional robotics approach: build models of the world, break the problem into perception, planning, and control, and engineer each piece carefully. Learning might help with a particular component, but it wasn’t necessarily the organizing principle.

The other mindset was gaining momentum from deep learning: could we learn much more of the behavior directly from data, perhaps even end to end? There was a lot of excitement about reinforcement learning and the possibility that robots could acquire skills through experience.

The tension was really about how much structure we should provide versus how much the robot should learn. And in robotics, that question immediately runs into practical constraints: collecting experience takes time, hardware breaks, and an approach that works in a controlled experiment may not generalize.

r001.rationale: The response describes a traditional, carefully engineered approach and a tension over how much structure to provide, but it does not clearly identify a prevailing view that systems should incorporate as much prior structure as possible.

r002.rationale: It mentions excitement about reinforcement learning and robots acquiring skills through experience, but does not say that robots were expected to learn by themselves or that this expectation led robotics researchers to disparage supervised learning.

sol-6.1.text:
Around 2017, there were roughly two camps. One believed we should learn everything end to end: take in pixels, output motor commands, and let data drive the whole system. Deep learning was doing so well in computer vision that there was a lot of excitement about bringing that approach into robotics.

The other camp was more skeptical. Robotics already had powerful tools for planning, control, and state estimation, and learning an entire system from scratch seemed inefficient and difficult to make reliable. From that perspective, learning should help with particular components, while we keep the structure we already understand.

That’s a simplified picture, but a lot of the discussion was about how much to learn and how much prior structure to build in.

r001.rationale: The response says the skeptical camp favored keeping existing structure and learning particular components, but it does not clearly identify a mindset of incorporating as much prior structure as possible.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention supervised learning being disparaged or an expectation that robots should learn by themselves.
